title: The Development of the Advertising Industry in New Zealand

paragraphs.text: The first advertising in New Zealand, apart from some very simple leaflets, was in the country’s early newspapers. In the 1840s these newspapers, mainly weeklies, rarely ran to more than four pages. Similar in size to today’s tabloids, the front and back pages were typically devoted to advertisements for building materials, women’s dresses and men’s suits to withstand the changeable weather, sheep imported from Australia and land for sale. These were immediate needs, not luxuries, and of more interest to readers than debates about political issues or outdated news from the other side of the world. At this time, advertising space was expensive and usually only featured brief headings. The laborious business of engraving onto wooden blocks in order to print meant that newspapers included hardly any illustrations, apart from such things as images of sailing vessels to accompany timetables showing the times of ship arrivals and departures. Newspapers in scattered coastal communities cooperated with their rivals, sharing news stories, taking subscriptions and re-directing advertising, all in a rather disorganised way. However, in the 1860s inland settlement of the country developed more quickly and the population grew. As a result, the first daily newspapers needed a more orderly approach to news gathering. This growth also provided significant opportunities for newspapers to increase their financial revenues through the sale of more advertising space. It has been claimed that New Zealand advertising agencies had their beginnings in 1891 when Charles Haines established his advertising business in Wellington. Haines’ company acted as the agent for a single local paper, the Wairarapa Daily News. Recent research, however, has shown that long before 1891 at least two advertising agents operated in the cities of Dunedin and Christchurch, although there are no records of these businesses by the beginning of the 20th century. Possibly the country’s first advertising agency was in fact Wheeler’s establishment, which promoted its services in the Southland Times as early as 1869. The Wheeler Advertising Agency described itself as an advertising and general commission agent. As well as being the advertising agent for a long list of newspapers and magazines, Mr Wheeler was also a real estate agent. There seem to be no records of him working in advertising after November 1885. The development of a professional advertising industry in New Zealand really got started in the late 19th century, when there was a revolution in printing techniques. The Evening Press in Wellington was, in the 1880s, one of the earliest daily newspapers to use the then new printing technology called lithography. This allowed the paper to regularly publish cartoons, which was an innovation in New Zealand. However, advertisers took surprisingly little advantage of the technological advances until the beginning of the 20th century, when agents like J Inglis Wright started to add a more professional look to advertisements and promotional material. However, most newspaper reproduction was still poor quality and this would remain a problem for decades. As a result, the more imaginative work was mainly produced for posters, which advertising agencies now started to create for their clients on a regular basis. By 1911 the advertising agency of J Ilott Ltd was employing a range of creative staff, including a small group of writers and a full-time artist who came from Australia. The same year the agency sent its clients a brochure showing how professional advertising could promote their products and improve profitability. Ilott’s also produced Cuts, a catalogue showing hundreds of illustrations that were designed to mainly appeal to shops, promoting the idea of moderately priced advertising. Around 1912 government funding started to become available to encourage employment in trades like advertising. As a result, some students were provided with training in skills associated with advertising such as lithography, print-making, drawing and lettering, in school for the first time. By now there was a growing acceptance of advertising by the business community. Evidence for this can be found in 1914 when a group of Auckland businesses, printing firms and advertising contractors under the chairmanship of I W Court formed an advertising club to promote the industry’s interests. Later that year it called for designers to draw up ideas for an official badge, for which a prize was awarded. This might have been the country’s first commercial design award. Advertising news now regularly featured in the press, which was only too happy to remind readers about the value of advertising. In 1927 the increasingly prominent role of advertising was highlighted when the industry organised a major New Zealand advertising exhibition that ran for five days in the Auckland Town Hall. Some of the design work was done by Carlton Studio, which would, within the next two years, become Carlton Carruthers Lets, and later a major advertising agency. Much later, from the mid-to-late 1940s, the industry also published a magazine, Deadline: The Adman’s Annual, which reported on industry news and developments. With this initiative it is possible to say that the era of the professional advertising industry in New Zealand had reached a high point.
